description: Precision AgriTech - Agronomic Advisory Knowledge Base. Covers all 33 plant-ml crop-disease classes across Tomato, Potato, Corn, Apple, Grape, Rice, and Cassava. Sourced from FAO, IRRI, IITA, CIAT, and University Extension services (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, UC Davis, Iowa State).

tomato/healthy.general_description: The tomato plant shows no signs of disease, pest damage, or nutritional deficiency. Foliage displays uniform deep green coloration with firm, turgid leaf tissue. Continue standard agronomic practice.
cultural_controls: Maintain adequate plant spacing (45–60 cm) to promote airflow and reduce humidity.
Monitor soil moisture and maintain consistent irrigation to avoid drought stress.
Rotate crops annually to prevent soilborne disease buildup.
Inspect plants weekly for early signs of pest or pathogen activity.
tomato/healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Continue routine field monitoring and maintain preventative spray calendar.
tomato/healthy.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

tomato/early_blight.general_description: Early Blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Characteristic concentric brown lesions with a target-like pattern appear on older, lower leaves first, progressing upward. Severe infections cause premature defoliation, reducing photosynthetic capacity and yield by 20–30%.
tomato/early_blight.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24–29°C), high relative humidity (>80%), extended leaf wetness (>6 hours), and alternating wet-dry cycles. Nitrogen-deficient plants are significantly more susceptible.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply every 7–10 days beginning at first sign of disease or during high-risk weather windows.
Apply preventatively before rain events or when humidity exceeds 80% for >6 hours.
Apply at first symptom appearance; do not exceed 3 applications per season to prevent resistance.
Apply as a protective spray every 10–14 days in humid conditions.

cultural_controls: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves immediately to reduce inoculum load.
Avoid overhead irrigation; switch to drip or furrow irrigation to minimize leaf wetness duration.
Apply nitrogen fertilization as split doses to maintain adequate plant nutrition and resistance.
Implement minimum 3-year crop rotation with non-Solanaceous crops.
Use certified disease-free transplants and resistant cultivars (e.g., Plum Regal, Mountain Magic).
Mulch the soil surface to prevent rain splash dispersal of soilborne conidia.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative mode of action; most effective when applied before disease onset.
Suppresses soilborne inoculum; combine with copper-based foliar sprays for integrated management.

tomato/early_blight.immediate_action: Remove all visibly infected lower leaves. Switch to drip irrigation immediately. Apply Mancozeb 80% WP or Chlorothalonil as a protective spray. Monitor daily for disease progression.
tomato/early_blight.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

tomato/late_blight.general_description: Late Blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans — the same pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine of 1845. Water-soaked, dark olive-green to brown lesions rapidly expand across leaves, stems, and fruits. A characteristic white cottony sporulation (sporangiophores) appears on the underside of infected tissue in humid conditions. Under favorable weather, entire crops can be destroyed within 1–2 weeks without intervention.
tomato/late_blight.favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (15–22°C), relative humidity >90%, extended leaf wetness (>10 hours), rain events followed by cool nights. Particularly severe in coastal and valley regions with persistent morning fog.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at first symptom appearance; repeat every 5–7 days under high disease pressure.
Apply within 24–48 hours of infection event; highly systemic.
Apply preventatively or immediately after a high-risk weather event.
Apply every 5–7 days as a protective barrier during high-risk periods.

cultural_controls: IMMEDIATELY isolate affected parcels — do not allow workers or equipment to pass through infected areas without decontamination.
Destroy all infected plant material by deep burial or incineration (do NOT compost).
Eliminate overhead irrigation; switch to drip irrigation only to eliminate foliar wetness.
Implement strict crop rotation — do not plant Solanaceous crops on affected land for 3+ years.
Monitor neighboring fields and report confirmed outbreaks to local agricultural authority.
Apply stramineous mulch to suppress soilborne sporangia splash-dispersal.
Plant certified blight-resistant cultivars (e.g., Defiant PhR, Mountain Merit).

biological_controls.notes: Preventative only; not effective on established infections. Use as part of an integrated spray program with copper-based fungicides.

tomato/late_blight.immediate_action: CRITICAL: Isolate affected perimeter immediately. Restrict all overhead irrigation. Apply a curative fungicide (Cymoxanil + Mancozeb or Dimethomorph) within 24 hours. Notify neighboring farm operators. Prepare contingency harvest of unaffected fruit if disease spread exceeds 30% canopy coverage.
tomato/late_blight.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

potato/healthy.general_description: The potato plant is in healthy condition with no visible signs of foliar disease, pest activity, or nutritional stress. Continue standard management practices.
cultural_controls: Use certified disease-free seed tubers from trusted suppliers.
Maintain adequate hilling to protect developing tubers from greening and late blight.
Monitor soil moisture to avoid waterlogging, which predisposes plants to Pythium and bacterial rot.
Scout fields weekly for early signs of aphid colonies (vectors of Potato Virus Y and PVX).
potato/healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Maintain preventative spray schedule based on Blight Forecasting models (e.g., BLITECAST) or regional disease alert systems.
potato/healthy.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

potato/early_blight.general_description: Potato Early Blight, caused by Alternaria solani, produces characteristic target-like concentric ring lesions on older lower leaves. Unlike Late Blight, lesions are dry and angular, often surrounded by a yellow chlorotic halo. The disease progresses upward as the season advances and accelerates under warm, humid conditions.
potato/early_blight.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24–29°C), high relative humidity (>80%), periods of dry weather alternating with rain, and nutrient-stressed plants (particularly nitrogen and potassium deficiency).

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply every 10–14 days starting at row closure (canopy closure).
Apply as a protective spray before expected rain events.
Apply at first symptom appearance; maximum 3 applications per season.

cultural_controls: Apply balanced NPK fertilization — adequate nitrogen and potassium significantly reduce susceptibility.
Remove heavily infected haulm tissue; do not leave in field after harvest.
Implement 3–4 year crop rotation with cereals or legumes.
Use certified seed tubers with known disease resistance.
Avoid overhead irrigation during evening hours to reduce nocturnal leaf wetness.

biological_controls.notes: Best applied preventatively at 7-day intervals; can be combined with conventional fungicide programs.

potato/early_blight.immediate_action: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves. Apply Mancozeb 80% WP or Chlorothalonil protectively. Ensure adequate potassium and nitrogen nutrition via leaf tissue test.
potato/early_blight.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

potato/late_blight.general_description: Potato Late Blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the most destructive potato disease worldwide. Pale green to brown water-soaked lesions appear on leaves and rapidly expand; white sporulation is visible on the underside of leaves in moist conditions. Infected stems collapse, and tubers develop brown, granular internal rot (storage rot). A single infected field can be completely destroyed within 7–10 days under epidemic conditions.
potato/late_blight.favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (10–20°C), prolonged relative humidity >90%, rain events, fog, and extended periods of leaf wetness (>10 hours). The pathogen survives in volunteer potato plants and infected tubers in storage or soil.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at first sign of disease or after a Blitecast warning threshold is exceeded; repeat every 7–14 days.
Apply preventatively or at very early infection; most effective before symptom expression.
Apply every 5–7 days during high-risk weather windows.

cultural_controls: IMMEDIATELY destroy or desiccate infected haulm (diquat or mechanical destruction) to prevent tuber infection.
Delay harvest by 2–3 weeks after haulm destruction to allow tuber skin set and reduce storage rot.
Never store or replant tubers from a blight-affected field.
Eliminate all volunteer potato plants in and around the field.
Implement a rigorous 4–5 year rotation; never plant potatoes after tomatoes.
Plant certified blight-resistant cultivars (e.g., Sarpo Mira, Penta, Innovator).

biological_controls.notes: Preventative use only as part of an integrated blight management program; pair with copper-based protectants.

potato/late_blight.immediate_action: CRITICAL: Begin haulm desiccation protocol on severely affected parcels immediately. Apply a systemic curative fungicide (Metalaxyl-M + Mancozeb) within 24 hours. Cease all irrigation. Alert neighboring potato growers. Check tuber lots in storage for early rot symptoms.
potato/late_blight.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

corn/healthy.general_description: The corn (maize) plant is in healthy condition with vibrant green foliage and no evidence of disease lesions, rust pustules, or foliar blight symptoms. Maintain current crop management practice.
cultural_controls: Monitor for European corn borer and western corn rootworm populations during silking.
Maintain adequate side-dress nitrogen applications at V6 growth stage.
Ensure adequate plant population density (70,000–90,000 plants/ha) for targeted hybrid.
Scout bi-weekly for early disease signs, particularly in late July/August when conditions favor rust and blight.
corn/healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Maintain preventative scouting program and weather-based disease monitoring.
corn/healthy.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

corn/common_rust.general_description: Common Rust, caused by Puccinia sorghi, is an obligate biotrophic fungus producing brick-red to cinnamon-colored urediniospore pustules on both leaf surfaces. Pustules rupture the epidermis and appear in dense clusters along leaf veins. Under severe infection, premature senescence and significant yield losses of 10–30% can occur, particularly in susceptible sweet corn cultivars and late-planted field corn.
corn/common_rust.favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (16–23°C), high relative humidity (>95%), extended periods of leaf wetness (dew periods), and cloudy overcast conditions. Urediospores are wind-dispersed over long distances from southern overwintering regions (tropical/subtropical rust nurseries).

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at VT (tasseling) to R2 (blister) growth stage when rust pustules first appear on upper leaves.
Apply from VT through R3 (milk) growth stage; maximum 2 applications per season.
Single application at VT or when rust first detected on ear leaf; highly effective on Puccinia spp.

cultural_controls: Plant rust-resistant hybrids — check seed catalog for Rp gene resistance ratings.
Time planting to avoid peak urediospore dispersal periods in late summer.
Monitor for rust progression from the bottom canopy upward — treatment is most economic at VT stage.
Maintain balanced NPK fertilization; potassium deficiency increases rust susceptibility.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative use; apply at early canopy development before rust season onset.

corn/common_rust.immediate_action: Scout the entire field for pustule density. If more than 30% of plants show pustules above the ear leaf at VT stage, apply a triazole or strobilurin-triazole combination fungicide within the next 3–5 days.
corn/common_rust.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

corn/northern_leaf_blight.general_description: Northern Leaf Blight (NLB), caused by Exserohilum turcicum, produces distinctive long, elliptical, tan to gray-green lesions (3–15 cm) that run parallel to leaf veins. The lesions have wavy borders and may develop a dark olivaceous sporulation (conidia) under moist conditions. NLB infection above the ear leaf during the grain-fill period (R1–R6) can cause yield losses of 30–50% in highly susceptible hybrids.
corn/northern_leaf_blight.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18–27°C), relative humidity >90%, extended periods of leaf wetness (>6 hours), and moderate rainfall. Disease is most severe in areas with minimum tillage and surface corn debris from previous crop.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at VT (tasseling) through R1 (silking); most critical application window for ear leaf protection.
Apply at VT stage when disease is detected in lower canopy; do not apply after R3 (milk).
Preventative-to-curative application at VT for highly susceptible hybrids in high-disease-risk regions.

cultural_controls: Plant NLB-resistant hybrids — look for Ht1, Ht2, Htm1 gene resistance in seed catalog.
Implement full-inversion plowing or minimum 2-year rotation to decompose infected surface debris.
Avoid planting corn on corn in regions with historically high NLB pressure.
Perform intensive scouting from V10 through R2 to evaluate economic threshold (approximately 50% plants with lesions above ear leaf).
Maintain adequate nitrogen and potassium fertilization to support plant immunity.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative supplemental application during early canopy development; not a replacement for conventional fungicides at VT in high-risk scenarios.

corn/northern_leaf_blight.immediate_action: Evaluate disease severity index (DSI) across the field. If >30% plants show NLB lesions on or above the ear leaf before R3, apply a strobilurin-triazole combination fungicide. Under high-risk conditions, a single well-timed VT application can protect yield potential significantly.
corn/northern_leaf_blight.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

apple/healthy.general_description: The apple tree foliage is in healthy condition with no visible scab lesions, rust pustules, or foliar disease symptoms. Maintain current integrated pest and disease management schedule.
cultural_controls: Implement a preventative copper fungicide program at green tip and pink bud stages before wet weather.
Prune trees annually during dormancy to improve light penetration and air circulation.
Remove and destroy mummified fruit and fallen leaves — primary inoculum sources for Venturia and Gymnosporangium.
Scout weekly from green tip through petal fall for early disease and pest signs.
Maintain soil pH 6.0–6.5 to optimize nutrient availability and plant health.
apple/healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Maintain scheduled spray program based on apple scab infection model (Mills periods) and regional pathogen pressure alerts.
apple/healthy.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

apple/cedar_apple_rust.general_description: Cedar Apple Rust is a heteroecious rust fungus requiring both apple (or crabapple) and eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) or other susceptible Juniperus species to complete its life cycle. Bright orange-yellow lesions (aecia) appear on the upper surface of apple leaves from petal fall through early summer, often with distinctive tube-like aeciospore horns on the lower leaf surface. Severely infected leaves may drop prematurely, weakening the tree and reducing fruit set in subsequent years.
apple/cedar_apple_rust.favorable_conditions: Wet spring weather with temperatures of 10–24°C during apple bloom and green tip stages. Orange gelatinous telial horns on cedar galls release basidiospores during warm spring rains that infect apple tissue. Orchards within 500 m of susceptible Juniper hosts are at highest risk.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply from silver tip through third cover (5–6 applications); most critical from pink to third cover when spore release peaks.
Apply at pink bud and repeat every 10–14 days through petal fall.
Apply from green tip through first cover as part of a multi-disease protectant program.
Apply at green tip; avoid use when temperatures exceed 32°C to prevent phytotoxicity.

cultural_controls: Remove or eradicate eastern red cedar and susceptible Juniperus hosts within 500 m of the orchard where feasible.
Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Enterprise, Liberty, Freedom, GoldRush).
Prune to improve airflow and reduce canopy humidity during spring infection periods.
Remove infected leaves and mummified fruit at season end to reduce local inoculum.
Monitor regional rust spore release forecasts from local extension services or weather-based models.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative use from green tip through petal fall; pair with sulfur or captan for adequate rust protection in organic systems.

apple/cedar_apple_rust.immediate_action: Apply a triazole fungicide (myclobutanil or tebuconazole) immediately if orange-yellow lesions are detected at or after petal fall. Inspect nearby Juniperus species for active telial horn galls and remove if feasible. Inform neighboring orchard operators of active rust pressure.
apple/cedar_apple_rust.sources: USDA ARS, University Extension bulletins (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue, Iowa State)

tomato/septoria_leaf_spot.general_description: Septoria leaf spot causes circular brown lesions with gray centers and black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) on lower leaves, leading to severe defoliation and sunscald.
tomato/septoria_leaf_spot.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (20–25°C), high humidity (>80%), and frequent rain or prolonged overhead irrigation.
tomato/septoria_leaf_spot.immediate_action: Prune severely diseased lower foliage; avoid overhead watering; apply protective fungicide.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at first sign of disease and repeat every 7–10 days under humid conditions.
Apply protectively before rain events.

cultural_controls: Mulch heavily around tomato base to suppress spore splashing from soil.
Space plants 60 cm apart and stake or trellis to maximize airflow.
Remove and destroy infected plant debris at end of season.
Rotate away from solanaceous crops for at least 2–3 years.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative biofungicide foliar spray applied prior to severe lesion development.

tomato/septoria_leaf_spot.sources: University of Maryland Extension - Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato; Purdue Extension BP-22-W

corn/gray_leaf_spot.general_description: Gray leaf spot causes rectangular tan-to-gray lesions restricted by leaf veins, coalescing under high humidity to blight entire corn leaves.
corn/gray_leaf_spot.favorable_conditions: Prolonged high humidity (>90%), warm temperatures (24–30°C), and extended overcast conditions with dew.
corn/gray_leaf_spot.immediate_action: Scout around tasseling; evaluate hybrid resistance; apply foliar fungicide if lesions appear on third leaf below ear before tasseling.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at VT/R1 growth stages if disease is present on lower leaves.

cultural_controls: Plant resistant maize hybrids.
Rotate with non-host crops (soybean, small grains) for 1–2 years.
Incorporate or manage corn residue to reduce overwintering fungal inoculum.

biological_controls.notes: Foliar biofungicide for fungal pathogen suppression.

corn/gray_leaf_spot.sources: Iowa State University Extension - Gray Leaf Spot; Purdue Extension BP-056-W

corn/northern_leaf_spot.general_description: Northern leaf spot (Helminthosporium carbonum) causes small circular or oblong tan lesions with concentric zones on corn leaves and ears.
corn/northern_leaf_spot.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18–27°C) and high humidity or frequent rainfall.
corn/northern_leaf_spot.immediate_action: Inspect inbred and hybrid stands; apply triazole or strobilurin fungicide if lesions progress rapidly.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at onset of lesion development prior to reproductive stage.

cultural_controls: Rotate out of corn for at least 1 year.
Till crop residue to facilitate decomposition in high-tillage systems.
Select certified resistant seed lines (Hm1 gene resistance).

biological_controls.notes: Early foliar suppression.

corn/northern_leaf_spot.sources: University of Illinois Field Crop Diseases - Northern Leaf Spot; CIMMYT Maize Guide

corn/maize_streak_virus.general_description: Maize streak virus causes continuous narrow chlorotic stripes along leaf veins, stunted plant growth, and severe failure of cob formation.
corn/maize_streak_virus.favorable_conditions: Warm climates (22–32°C) favoring populations of leafhopper vectors (Cicadulina mbila).
corn/maize_streak_virus.immediate_action: Rogue out early-infected plants; spray leafhopper vectors; avoid overlapping staggered plantings.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Seed dressing prior to sowing to protect seedlings against leafhoppers for 3–4 weeks.

cultural_controls: Plant MSV-resistant hybrid varieties certified by regional seed agencies.
Establish a crop-free host period to disrupt leafhopper lifecycles.
Clear grass weeds around field perimeters that host vector leafhoppers.

biological_controls.notes: Entomopathogenic fungus targeting leafhopper vectors.

corn/maize_streak_virus.sources: CIMMYT / IITA Maize Streak Virus Monograph; FAO IPM Guidelines

corn/maize_lethal_necrosis.general_description: Maize lethal necrosis (MLN) results from co-infection of MCMV and SCMV/MDMV, causing severe leaf chlorosis, deadheart, necrotic drying, and total ear failure.
corn/maize_lethal_necrosis.favorable_conditions: Continuous overlapping maize production in warm regions with presence of thrips and beetle vectors.
corn/maize_lethal_necrosis.immediate_action: Quarantine affected field; rogue and bury infected plants; enforce strict maize-free fallow period.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Seed dressing to prevent vector transmission by corn thrips.

cultural_controls: Enforce a mandatory maize-free break for at least 2 full months across the production zone.
Plant only certified virus-free commercial hybrid seed; do not replant saved grain.
Rotate with non-poaceous crops (legumes, cassava, sunflower) for at least 2 seasons.

biological_controls.notes: Botanical antifeedant to deter thrips and beetle vectors.

corn/maize_lethal_necrosis.sources: CIMMYT - Maize Lethal Necrosis Management Manual; FAO / KALRO Technical Guidance

apple/scab.general_description: Apple scab causes olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit, causing leaf distortion, premature leaf drop, and cracked scabby fruit.
apple/scab.favorable_conditions: Cool, wet spring weather (15–24°C) with prolonged leaf wetness exceeding Mills infection periods (6–9 hours).
apple/scab.immediate_action: Apply protective or kickback fungicide within the infection window; shred fallen orchard leaf litter.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply preventatively from green tip through petal fall prior to forecasted rain events.
Post-infection curative spray applied within 72 hours of rain infection event.

cultural_controls: Mow and shred fallen autumn leaves or apply 5% urea spray to speed up leaf breakdown.
Prune tree canopy annually to facilitate rapid drying of foliage after dew and rain.
Plant scab-resistant cultivars (Liberty, GoldRush, Enterprise).

biological_controls.notes: Preventative biofungicide spray during pre-bloom and bloom periods.

apple/scab.sources: Cornell Cooperative Extension - Apple Scab; Penn State Tree Fruit Production Guide

apple/frog_eye_leaf_spot.general_description: Frog eye leaf spot causes small circular lesions with purple margins and tan/white centers, accompanied by black rot cankers on branches and mummified fruit.
apple/frog_eye_leaf_spot.favorable_conditions: Warm, wet conditions (20–27°C) with rain splashes distributing fungal conidia from cankers.
apple/frog_eye_leaf_spot.immediate_action: Prune dead wood and mummified fruit; apply protective broad-spectrum fungicide from tight cluster through cover sprays.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at petal fall and cover sprays every 10–14 days.

cultural_controls: Prune and burn dead twigs, cankered limbs, and mummified apples during winter.
Prune cankered wood at least 15 cm below infected margins.
Maintain tree health and avoid herbicide or winter injury that creates entry wounds.

biological_controls.notes: Suppressive biological spray during early leaf expansion.

apple/frog_eye_leaf_spot.sources: University of Kentucky Extension PPA-34 - Frog Eye Leaf Spot; Penn State Fruit Pathology

apple/powdery_mildew.general_description: Powdery mildew produces white powdery felt on young shoots, leaves, and buds, causing leaf curling, stunted shoot growth, and fruit russeting.
apple/powdery_mildew.favorable_conditions: High relative humidity (70–95%) without rain, and moderate temperatures (18–25°C). Free water actually inhibits spore germination.
apple/powdery_mildew.immediate_action: Prune out white 'silver shoot' tips; apply sulfur or systemic triazole fungicide at tight cluster through petal fall.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply every 7–10 days from pink bud; do not apply when temperatures exceed 28°C.
Apply at bloom and petal fall for systemic kickback control.

cultural_controls: Manually cut out infected silver shoot tips during dormant and spring pruning.
Avoid excess nitrogen applications that stimulate late vegetative flushes.
Select resistant varieties (e.g. Honeycrisp, Gala).

biological_controls.notes: Biological preventative spray for powdery mildew suppression.

apple/powdery_mildew.sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit - Apple Powdery Mildew; UC IPM Apple Guidelines

grape/healthy.general_description: Grapevine foliage displays uniform dark green color, healthy lobed margins, vigorous shoot tips, and no foliar lesions.
grape/healthy.immediate_action: No treatment required. Maintain canopy management and preventative fungicide schedule.
cultural_controls: Manage shoot positioning and cluster zone airflow.
Maintain vineyard floor cover crop to control soil moisture.
grape/healthy.sources: UC Davis Viticulture & Enology; Cornell Grape Pathology

grape/esca.general_description: Esca (black measles) causes characteristic interveinal 'tiger-stripe' necrosis on leaves, spotted berries, and vascular dieback in mature vines.
grape/esca.favorable_conditions: Fungal entry via winter pruning wounds; symptoms flare during high-temperature water stress in mid-summer.
grape/esca.immediate_action: Tag symptomatic vines for delayed remedial pruning; protect pruning wounds with fungicide or sealant; avoid summer vine stress.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Spray or paint onto dormant pruning cuts within 24 hours of cutting.

cultural_controls: Practice late winter delayed pruning when cuts heal rapidly.
Apply wound sealant to large cuts (>1.5 cm diameter).
Train a new basal sucker to replace affected trunks (trunk renewal).
Disinfect pruning shears regularly between vines.

biological_controls.notes: Bio-protectant applied directly to pruning cuts to colonize wounds against trunk fungi.

grape/esca.sources: UC IPM Grapevine Trunk Diseases: Esca; INRAE Grapevine Trunk Diseases Guide

grape/downy_mildew.general_description: Downy mildew causes yellowish translucent 'oil spots' on the upper leaf surface and dense white sporulation on the underside, defoliating vines rapidly.
grape/downy_mildew.favorable_conditions: Spring 10-10-10 rule: 10 mm rainfall, 10°C temperature, and 10 cm shoot growth; relative humidity >90%.
grape/downy_mildew.immediate_action: Apply protective or systemic oomycete fungicide before rain; maintain open cluster zone canopy.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply preventatively or early post-infection during warm wet periods.
Protectant spray prior to forecasted rain events.

cultural_controls: Pull leaves around grape clusters to accelerate drying after rain.
Maintain good vineyard soil drainage to eliminate standing puddles.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative biofungicide spray during active shoot growth.

grape/downy_mildew.sources: Cornell Viticulture - Grape Downy Mildew; UC Davis IPM Grape Downy Mildew

rice/healthy.general_description: Rice leaves show uniform erect green blades, healthy tillering, and no discoloration or lesions.
rice/healthy.immediate_action: Maintain optimal water depth and balanced fertilizer application.
cultural_controls: Maintain balanced N-P-K fertilizer split.
Ensure uniform field leveling and water circulation.
rice/healthy.sources: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank; FAO Rice Production Systems

rice/blast.general_description: Rice blast produces diamond-shaped or spindle-shaped lesions with gray centers and dark brown borders, causing extensive leaf death and neck rot.
rice/blast.favorable_conditions: High relative humidity (>90%), moderate temperatures (20–28°C), prolonged dew wetness (>10h), and excessive nitrogen application.
rice/blast.immediate_action: Drain field temporarily if excess nitrogen was applied; apply blast-specific fungicide immediately at tillering/booting.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at early tillering and heading to protect panicle neck.
Apply at first sign of spindle lesions.

cultural_controls: Avoid excess nitrogen applications; balance with potassium and silicon.
Maintain continuous water depth (5–10 cm) to suppress blast sporulation.
Plant certified blast-resistant cultivars.
Destroy infected straw and stubble after harvest.

biological_controls.notes: Seed and foliar biofungicide application.

rice/blast.sources: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank - Blast; PhilRice Blast Compendium

rice/brown_spot.general_description: Brown spot causes oval, dark brown spots with yellow halos across rice leaves and glumes, severely reducing grain quality in nutrient-deficient soils.
rice/brown_spot.favorable_conditions: High humidity (>85%), temperatures 25–30°C, and nutrient-deficient soils (especially lacking potassium, silicon, or zinc).
rice/brown_spot.immediate_action: Apply balanced potassium fertilizer; correct soil nutrient deficiencies; apply foliar fungicide if spreading.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply protectively at early tillering and panicle initiation.

cultural_controls: Apply balanced N-P-K fertilizer and supplement with potassium and zinc.
Soak seeds in warm water (52–54°C for 15 min) prior to sowing.
Avoid prolonged dry spells in the paddy.

biological_controls.notes: Foliar spray for Bipolaris suppression.

rice/brown_spot.sources: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank - Brown Spot; University of Arkansas Rice Diseases

rice/bacterial_leaf_blight.general_description: Bacterial leaf blight causes wavy water-soaked stripes starting at leaf tips and margins, rapidly turning yellow-white with milky bacterial ooze beads.
rice/bacterial_leaf_blight.favorable_conditions: High temperatures (25–34°C), relative humidity >80%, and driving monsoon storms causing leaf abrasion.
rice/bacterial_leaf_blight.immediate_action: Drain excess standing water; withhold nitrogen fertilizer top-dressing; avoid damaging leaves during weeding.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at first sign of yellow marginal lesions.

cultural_controls: Stop nitrogen top-dressing during disease flare-up.
Ensure good field drainage during heavy rains.
Eradicate weed hosts (Leersia hexandra) along paddy bunds.
Plant resistant cultivars (Xa gene lines).

biological_controls.notes: Biological antagonism against Xanthomonas.

rice/bacterial_leaf_blight.sources: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank - Bacterial Blight; FAO Rice IPM Pathology

rice/tungro.scientific_name: Rice tungro spherical virus + Rice tungro bacilliform virus
rice/tungro.general_description: Tungro disease causes leaf yellowing or orange discoloration starting from tips, severe plant stunting, delayed flowering, and sterile panicles.
rice/tungro.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24–30°C) supporting population outbreaks of green leafhopper vector (Nephotettix virescens).
rice/tungro.immediate_action: Plow under heavily infected fields; control leafhopper vectors; synchronize planting dates across the canal command area.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Foliar spray to suppress green leafhopper vectors upon detection.

cultural_controls: Synchronize planting dates within 2–3 weeks across irrigation blocks.
Observe a 30-day crop-free fallow between successive crops.
Plant tungro-resistant certified rice varieties (Matatag lines).
Rogue and destroy infected hills within first 30 days.

biological_controls.notes: Targeted bio-insecticide for green leafhopper vectors.

rice/tungro.sources: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank - Tungro Disease; PhilRice Technical Bulletin

rice/hispa.general_description: Rice hispa adults scrape green tissue leaving white parallel streaks; internal leaf-mining grubs tunnel through leaf tissue causing blighted leaves.
rice/hispa.favorable_conditions: Warm, humid conditions (>80% RH, 24–30°C) and heavy nitrogen fertilizer use.
rice/hispa.immediate_action: Net and destroy adult spiny beetles; clip leaf tips of seedlings before transplanting; spray contact insecticide if threshold exceeded.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply when adult hispa counts exceed 1–2 per hill.

cultural_controls: Clip seedling leaf tips before transplanting to eliminate eggs.
Sweep fields with hand nets to catch adult spiny beetles.
Avoid excessive nitrogen applications.
Drain paddies for 2–3 days to suppress larval development.

biological_controls.notes: Egg parasitoid release against hispa eggs.

rice/hispa.sources: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank - Rice Hispa; Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)

cassava/healthy.general_description: Cassava leaves show vibrant green palmate foliage with no mosaic mottle, vein distortion, necrosis, or mite feeding chlorosis.
cassava/healthy.immediate_action: Maintain weed control and monitor for whitefly vectors.
cultural_controls: Select clean stem cuttings from vigorous plants.
Keep field free of weed hosts.
cassava/healthy.sources: IITA Cassava Guide; FAO Save and Grow: Cassava

cassava/mosaic.general_description: Cassava mosaic disease causes severe yellow-green chlorotic mottling, leaf distortion, stunting, and up to 80% tuber yield reduction.
cassava/mosaic.favorable_conditions: Warm conditions (25–32°C) favoring high populations of Bemisia tabaci whitefly vectors.
cassava/mosaic.immediate_action: Rogue out and burn mosaic-stunted plants; use only CMD-resistant stem cuttings; control whitefly vector.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Foliar application to reduce whitefly vectors during early vegetative growth.

cultural_controls: Plant certified CMD-resistant cassava varieties (e.g. TME 419, TMS 98/0505).
Take cuttings only from completely symptom-free parent plants.
Rogue infected plants within the first 3 months of planting.
Isolate young plantations from older infected cassava fields.

biological_controls.notes: Botanical spray to repel whitefly vectors.

cassava/mosaic.sources: IITA Cassava Mosaic Disease Field Guide; FAO Integrated Cassava Management

cassava/brown_streak.general_description: Cassava brown streak causes feathery chlorosis along secondary leaf veins, brown streaks on green stems, and destructive dry-corky root rot.
cassava/brown_streak.favorable_conditions: Warm low-to-mid elevation zones (25–33°C) with persistent Bemisia tabaci whitefly pressure.
cassava/brown_streak.immediate_action: Quarantine field; destroy diseased plants; harvest roots early before rot spreads; never take cuttings from infected plants.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Foliar spray against sap-sucking whitefly vectors.

cultural_controls: Plant clean, certified tissue-culture planting material.
Enforce strict quarantine on movement of vegetative cassava cuttings.
Harvest roots early (at 8–9 months) before severe internal necrosis develops.
Rogue plants displaying vein feathery chlorosis and brown stem streaks.

biological_controls.notes: Entomopathogenic fungus targeting whitefly nymphs.

cassava/brown_streak.sources: IITA Cassava Brown Streak Disease Control Manual; FAO Plant Production and Protection Paper

cassava/green_mite.general_description: Cassava green mite feeds on young leaves causing yellow pinhead speckling, leaf narrowing, shoe-stringing, and shoot tip dieback.
cassava/green_mite.favorable_conditions: Hot, dry conditions (28–35°C, RH <65%) during extended dry seasons.
cassava/green_mite.immediate_action: Introduce predatory mites (Typhlodromalus aripo); avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays; apply selective acaricide if defoliation is severe.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Targeted acaricide application during severe dry season infestation.

cultural_controls: Plant early with start of rainy season so canopy matures before dry season.
Plant cultivars with hairy apical leaves that deter mite feeding.
Intercrop with maize or pigeon pea to reduce mite migration.

biological_controls.notes: Predatory phytoseiid mite that controls cassava green mite naturally.

cassava/green_mite.sources: IITA Biological Control of Cassava Green Mite; CIAT Cassava Pest Management

cassava/bacterial_blight.general_description: Cassava bacterial blight causes angular water-soaked leaf spots, leaf wilting, shoot dieback, and gummy exudate droplets along stems.
cassava/bacterial_blight.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (25–30°C) with high humidity and driving rainstorms creating leaf wounds.
cassava/bacterial_blight.immediate_action: Prune wilted shoot tips and burn them; disinfect tools; prune back stems in dry season; apply copper barrier before heavy rains.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at the onset of rainy season prior to storm events.

cultural_controls: Use certified disease-free stem cuttings.
Sterilize cutting tools in 10% bleach solution between plants.
Prune infected branches 20 cm below the lowest visible lesion.
Rotate fields with non-host crops (maize, sorghum, cowpea).

biological_controls.notes: Foliar bio-bactericide for Xanthomonas suppression.

cassava/bacterial_blight.sources: CIAT Cassava Bacterial Blight Manual; IITA Integrated Control of CBB in Africa
